title: Market Baseline
text:
Functional Role Segmentation
Individual job titles in the sample are highly fragmented, with many titles appearing only once. To identify broader hiring patterns, the titles are grouped into functional categories based on the primary focus of each role. This provides a more interpretable view of the types of analytics work represented in the selected apparel and fashion job postings.


Code
import plotly.express as px


def classify_role(title):
    title = str(title).lower()

    if any(keyword in title for keyword in [
        "business intelligence",
        "data analyst",
        "data governance",
        "data analytics"
    ]):
        return "BI / Data Analytics"

    elif any(keyword in title for keyword in [
        "operations",
        "operational",
        "region operations"
    ]):
        return "Operations Analytics"

    elif any(keyword in title for keyword in [
        "marketing",
        "media",
        "customer",
        "consumer",
        "digital analytics"
    ]):
        return "Marketing / Customer Analytics"

    elif any(keyword in title for keyword in [
        "merchandising",
        "merchandise",
        "ecommerce",
        "e-commerce",
        "retail",
        "wholesale",
        "sales planning"
    ]):
        return "Merchandising / Ecommerce"

    elif any(keyword in title for keyword in [
        "finance",
        "financial",
        "fp&a",
        "strategy",
        "strategic"
    ]):
        return "Finance / Strategy Analytics"

    elif any(keyword in title for keyword in [
        "product",
        "engineering"
    ]):
        return "Product / Engineering Analytics"

    else:
        return "Other Analytics"


# Create broader functional role categories
clean_df["ROLE_SEGMENT"] = clean_df["TITLE_CLEAN"].apply(classify_role)

# Count postings within each functional area
role_segment_counts = (
    clean_df["ROLE_SEGMENT"]
    .value_counts()
    .reset_index()
)

role_segment_counts.columns = [
    "Functional Area",
    "Number of Job Postings"
]

# Sort so the horizontal chart reads from smaller to larger values
role_segment_counts = role_segment_counts.sort_values(
    "Number of Job Postings",
    ascending=True
)

# Display counts for validation
print(role_segment_counts)

# Check whether any titles remain uncategorized
print("\nTitles classified as Other Analytics:")

other_titles = clean_df.loc[
    clean_df["ROLE_SEGMENT"] == "Other Analytics",
    "TITLE_CLEAN"
]

if len(other_titles) == 0:
    print("None")
else:
    print(other_titles.to_string(index=False))

# Create interactive Plotly chart
fig_role_segments = px.bar(
    role_segment_counts,
    x="Number of Job Postings",
    y="Functional Area",
    orientation="h",
    template="plotly_white",
    color_discrete_sequence=["#2C6E8C"],
    title="Job Postings by Functional Analytics Area"
)

fig_role_segments.update_layout(
    title_x=0.5,
    height=450,
    xaxis_title="Number of Job Postings",
    yaxis_title="Functional Area"
)

fig_role_segments.update_xaxes(
    dtick=1
)

fig_role_segments.show()

2        Merchandising / Ecommerce                       3

The functional segmentation shows that BI and data analytics roles represent the largest share of the selected sample, with 6 of the 19 postings. Marketing and customer analytics follows closely with 5 postings, while merchandising and ecommerce account for 3. Finance and strategy analytics and operations analytics each contribute 2 postings, and product or engineering analytics contributes 1.
This broader grouping reveals that analytics hiring within the selected apparel and fashion sample is distributed across several business functions rather than being concentrated in a single type of role. Because the dataset is small and the categories are derived from job-title wording, the results should be interpreted as a descriptive view of the selected postings rather than a standardized representation of the broader industry.

text:
Salary Distribution
Salary information is incomplete in the filtered dataset. Only postings with an originally reported salary range are included in this analysis. Missing salaries that were filled during data preparation are excluded so that the results reflect observed compensation information rather than imputed values.


Code
import pandas as pd
import plotly.graph_objects as go

salary_df = raw_df.copy()

salary_df["SALARY_FROM"] = pd.to_numeric(
    salary_df["SALARY_FROM"],
    errors="coerce"
)

salary_df["SALARY_TO"] = pd.to_numeric(
    salary_df["SALARY_TO"],
    errors="coerce"
)

salary_observed = salary_df.dropna(
    subset=["SALARY_FROM", "SALARY_TO"]
).copy()

salary_observed["SALARY_MIDPOINT"] = (
    salary_observed["SALARY_FROM"] +
    salary_observed["SALARY_TO"]
) / 2

salary_observed = salary_observed.sort_values(
    "SALARY_MIDPOINT"
).reset_index(drop=True)

# Build base label using title and employer
salary_observed["BASE_LABEL"] = salary_observed.apply(
    lambda row: (
        f"{row['TITLE_CLEAN']} ({row['COMPANY_NAME']})"
        if pd.notna(row.get("COMPANY_NAME"))
        else row["TITLE_CLEAN"]
    ),
    axis=1
)

# Number repeated labels so separate postings remain visible
salary_observed["DUPLICATE_NUMBER"] = (
    salary_observed.groupby("BASE_LABEL").cumcount() + 1
)

salary_observed["DUPLICATE_TOTAL"] = (
    salary_observed.groupby("BASE_LABEL")["BASE_LABEL"].transform("count")
)

salary_observed["LABEL"] = salary_observed.apply(
    lambda row: (
        f"{row['BASE_LABEL']} - Posting {row['DUPLICATE_NUMBER']}"
        if row["DUPLICATE_TOTAL"] > 1
        else row["BASE_LABEL"]
    ),
    axis=1
)

print(
    f"Postings with observed salary ranges: "
    f"{len(salary_observed)} of {len(raw_df)}"
)

fig = go.Figure()

for _, row in salary_observed.iterrows():

    fig.add_trace(
        go.Scatter(
            x=[
                row["SALARY_FROM"],
                row["SALARY_TO"]
            ],
            y=[
                row["LABEL"],
                row["LABEL"]
            ],
            mode="lines+markers",
            line=dict(width=4),
            marker=dict(size=9),
            showlegend=False,
            hovertemplate=(
                "<b>%{y}</b><br>"
                "Salary: $%{x:,.0f}"
                "<extra></extra>"
            )
        )
    )

fig.update_layout(
    title="Observed Salary Ranges",
    xaxis_title="Annual Salary ($)",
    yaxis_title="",
    height=560,
    margin=dict(
        l=320,
        r=40,
        t=70,
        b=50
    )
)

    tickprefix="$",
    tickformat="~s"
)

fig.show()

Only 4 of the 19 postings contain an observed salary range, so the salary findings should be interpreted cautiously. The available postings show variation in both the lower and upper ends of reported compensation, but the small number of observations is not sufficient to characterize salary levels across the full selected apparel and fashion analytics market. The chart therefore presents only compensation that was explicitly reported in the source postings.

title: Market Baseline
text:
Baseline Summary
The market baseline provides a descriptive snapshot of analytics-related opportunities within the selected apparel and fashion industry scope. The final dataset contains 19 verified job postings and shows that analytics work appears across several functional areas, including business intelligence, merchandising, ecommerce, finance, operations, and marketing.
Hiring activity is concentrated among a small group of employers and locations. Vuori and TJX each account for 5 postings, while California and Massachusetts each account for 5 postings. New York and Oregon also represent notable hiring locations within the sample.
Several variables have substantial missing information. Only 4 postings contain observed salary ranges, 9 contain recorded minimum experience requirements, and 4 contain an identifiable work arrangement. These limitations are retained explicitly in the analysis rather than treating imputed or missing values as if they were directly reported by employers.
Overall, the findings should be interpreted as a baseline for this narrowly defined apparel and fashion analytics market rather than as estimates of the broader analytics labor market. The results provide a foundation for the later skill-gap and career-evaluation stages of the project.

title: Career Evaluation
text: The 19 postings in our filtered dataset do not represent equally strong opportunities for this team. Some ask for skills our team has already demonstrated. Some are more attainable given their experience requirements. Some come from employers that are hiring repeatedly for comparable roles. A posting that scores well on one of these factors and poorly on another is a different kind of opportunity than one that scores well on all three, so judging postings one at a time misses that distinction.

title: Career Evaluation
text:
How We Define Opportunity
We treat a posting as a strong opportunity when it is attainable, relevant to skills our team already has, and backed by an employer that is actively hiring for similar work. These three factors come from what the market baseline and skill gap analysis already showed matters for this team, and the numbers behind each one explain why none of them can be skipped.
Attainability. Experience requirements in our sample are not evenly spread. 17 of the 19 postings list a minimum of 0 years of experience, and only 2 list a 5-year minimum. Accessibility is not a broad gradient across the sample, it is mostly uniform with a couple of high-bar outliers, which is exactly the kind of pattern a single accessibility score needs to flag rather than average away.
Skill relevance. We counted how many of our team’s four strongest self-rated skills (Data Analysis, Microsoft Excel, Stakeholder Management, Project Management) show up in each posting’s listed skills. 8 of the 19 postings match none of them, 7 match exactly one, and 4 match two. Not a single posting in our sample matches three or four. That spread means skill relevance genuinely separates the postings in our sample, almost half show no overlap at all with what our team already does well.
Employer signal. Vuori accounts for 5 of the 19 postings. TJX, counting its two listed company names together, also accounts for 5. Adidas accounts for 3. Together those three employers make up 13 of our 19 postings, 68%, while the remaining six employers in the sample post once each. An employer repeating a role is a different kind of signal than an employer posting once, and that 68% concentration is why employer signal carries real weight in the score.
None of these factors alone tells the full story. A role can be highly accessible but ask for skills our team lacks. A role can match our skills well but come from an employer with no other postings in our sample, making it a less repeatable target. Looking at all three together is what turns 19 individual postings into a ranked set of targets.

Where the Scoring Happens

title: Data Preparation
text:
Note on Sample Size
The final cleaned dataset contains 19 job postings. This reflects a known limitation of NAICS-based industry classification: many analytics roles at apparel/retail companies are tagged under unrelated NAICS codes rather than under clothing retail codes specifically. In our raw dataset, NAICS 458 alone matched only 18 of 504,208 postings, confirming this is not a minor edge case. To compensate, this dataset combines NAICS 458 (Clothing, Clothing Accessories, Shoe, and Jewelry Retailers) with an exact-match list of known apparel/fashion company names, then filters to narrow analyst job titles (business analyst, data analyst). The resulting sample size is small but each row is a verified, legitimate match.

title: Final Analytics
text:
Our filtered dataset has only 19 postings. Usable salary data exists for 4 of them. Usable experience data exists for 9 (see Market Baseline). That is too little consistent data to train and validate a regression or classification model without drawing conclusions from a handful of records, so instead of fitting a statistical model to data that cannot support one, our team built the Opportunity Score: a weighted, rule-based scoring model that ranks every posting in the sample using the three fields with strong coverage across all 19 records. This is a deliberate modeling choice, not a workaround. A regression or classifier trained on 19 rows, 4 of which have salary, would overfit and produce confident-looking numbers that mean nothing; a transparent, equal-weighted scoring model is the model that actually fits data this size. Salary and remote status are kept as separate context instead of being folded into the score, since folding in a field only 4 postings report would let those 4 records drive the ranking for the other 15.
Each of the 19 postings gets an Opportunity Score built from three component scores.

Skill fit score (0 to 4): how many of our team’s four self-rated strongest skills (Data Analysis, Microsoft Excel, Stakeholder Management, Project Management, from the Skill Gap Analysis) show up in that posting’s listed skills.
Accessibility score (0 to 3): a tiered score based on minimum years of experience required. A 0 year requirement scores highest. The score drops as the requirement climbs.
Employer signal score (1 to 5): the number of postings from that same employer in our sample. It is a proxy for how actively that company is hiring for this kind of role.

Salary and work arrangement were left out of the score. Only 4 of the 19 postings have usable data for each. Scoring on fields that sparse would let a handful of postings with reported data drive the ranking for the other 15. Market Baseline reports those two fields separately instead.
The three components carry equal weight. Our team had no outcome data, like actual application or offer results, to fit weights against instead. The employer signal score is not capped the same way the other two are. It is a raw count, and it currently ranges from 1 to 5 across our employers. That means an employer with many repeat postings can move the total by more per point than a skill fit or accessibility point can. Read the Opportunity Score alongside its three components, not as a single number on its own. That is why all three columns stay visible in the table below.

Code
import pandas as pd

df = pd.read_csv("data/processed/apparel_analyst_clean.csv")

team_strong_skills = ["Data Analysis", "Microsoft Excel", "Stakeholder Management", "Project Management"]

def skill_fit_score(skills_text):
    if pd.isna(skills_text):
        return 0
    matches = 0
    for strong in team_strong_skills:
        if strong.lower() in str(skills_text).lower():
            matches += 1
    return matches

df["SKILL_FIT_SCORE"] = df["SKILLS_LIST"].apply(skill_fit_score)

def accessibility_score(years):
    if years == 0:
        return 3
    elif years <= 2:
        return 2
    elif years <= 5:
        return 1
    else:
        return 0

df["ACCESSIBILITY_SCORE"] = df["MIN_YEARS_EXPERIENCE"].apply(accessibility_score)

employer_counts = df["COMPANY_NAME"].value_counts()
df["EMPLOYER_SIGNAL_SCORE"] = df["COMPANY_NAME"].map(employer_counts)

Scoring Model Diagnostics
A rule-based scoring model still needs to be checked, not just described. title: Final Analytics
text:
What the Scores Show
Vuori appears four times in the top six rows. This is a direct result of how often the company posts similar roles in our dataset, not a fluke of the scoring method. That repetition is what the employer signal score is meant to capture: a company hiring repeatedly for related work is a more realistic target than one with a single listing. The Sr. Manager, Ecommerce Analytics role at Vuori sits at the top of the list because it combines that hiring pattern with a moderate skill overlap and a low experience bar.
Adidas’ Manager, Digital Marketing Analytics role is the strongest non-Vuori result, driven mainly by skill fit rather than employer signal, since Adidas appears less often in the filtered postings. A role can score well either because it closely matches skills our team already has, or because the employer is clearly hiring at volume. Those are different types of opportunity. A few roles near the bottom of the list, like the TJX and Foot Locker postings, score lower mainly on skill fit, which lines up with the gaps found in the skill-gap analysis rather than a lack of accessibility or employer activity.

title: Final Analytics
text:
Evaluating the Score
Vuori and TJX, the two employers the scorecard ranks highest, are also the two employers with the most postings in Market Baseline. Low skill fit scores line up with the gaps found in the Skill Gap Analysis: Power BI, SQL, and Python. The scorecard has not been checked against real hiring outcomes. Use it to prioritize search and skill building, not to predict who gets an offer.

title: Career Pathway and Industry Scope
text:
Research Rationale
Business and data analysts turn operational data into decisions organizations can act on. Apparel retail is a good place to study that work, since retailers are constantly reacting to seasonal demand, shifting consumer preferences, inventory limits, pricing calls, and supply chain pressure. Those conditions give analytical skills a direct, visible role in how the business runs.
For a student weighing an analytics career, it is not always obvious which skills employers actually care about, or whether their coursework and experience line up with what the job market expects. A title like “business analyst” or “data analyst” hides a lot of variation: some mix of technical ability, analytical thinking, communication, and business judgment, and the exact mix shifts by employer. This project tries to pin down which skills matter most for business/data analyst roles in apparel retail specifically, then checks that list against our own team’s current skills.
That is what separates this from a plain labor-market summary: it is meant to work as a career evaluation tool. A student should be able to look at it and see what employers are asking for, where their own strengths already line up, and what still needs work before they apply.

title: Career Pathway and Industry Scope
text:
Literature Review
Umamaheswaran et al. (2023) looked at what employers ask for in business analytics postings and found a consistent mix: big data, business intelligence, and analytical technique on one side, communication and stakeholder management on the other. That matters for how we think about readiness. Knowing the software is not enough on its own; an analyst also has to understand the business problem and explain results to people who are not going to read the code.
Alshameri & Adhikari (2025) looked at business job postings the same way and identified the same kind of gap. Employers ask for a mix of general tools like Microsoft Office and data visualization plus skills specific to their field and the exact mix depends on industry and location. The study refers to this as a growing disconnect between what schools teach and what employers are actually looking for. In addition Debortoli et al. (2014) conducted a comparable analysis of business intelligence and big data postings and found the same pattern. Employers separate technical tool skills from broader analytical thinking and the strongest candidates show both.
Apparel retail is a fitting test case for that combination. Forecasting, inventory, pricing, and supply chain decisions all show up as recurring analytical needs in clothing retail, and IBISWorld (2025) backs that up with broader industry context on clothing and clothing accessory retailers. Demand in this sector moves fast and shifts with the seasons, which is part of why data-supported decisions carry more weight here than they might in a slower-moving industry.
Fashion retail has been leaning harder into data analytics in recent years. Oh (2020) found that fashion brands increasingly use data analytics to personalize products plan merchandising and improve profitability and argued that education has not kept pace with this shift. That gap between what the industry needs and what students are taught is part of what this project is looking to measure directly.
Retail hiring overall backs up the case for treating analytics as its own career path within the industry. The Planet Group (2025) found that retail hiring has gotten more selective even as it leans harder into technology, analytics, and customer experience. So while fewer people may be getting hired overall, the analytical roles that support pricing, inventory, operations, and customer decisions do not seem to be losing ground.
Job postings themselves give a more concrete look at what these roles ask for. Scanning ZipRecruiter listings, SQL, Excel, and a visualization tool like Tableau or Power BI show up repeatedly, alongside the usual asks for analytical and communication skills (ZipRecruiter, 2026b). We are treating this as a starting point rather than a finding, since individual job postings vary a lot by employer, seniority, and timing.
The same postings also show a fair amount of spread in pay and remote availability (ZipRecruiter, 2026a). Salary and remote work are not the central question we are asking, but they are useful context for judging how attractive a given role is. Once we are working with the MET Employability Career Match data, we will be able to check whether these early patterns hold up within our apparel retail scope specifically.
The demand for this kind of work is also reflected in national labor data. The U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics projects 7% growth for market research analyst roles from 2025 to 2035 well above the average for all occupations with a median annual wage of $78,760 as of May 2025 (U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics, 2025). The core skills the Bureau lists are analytical thinking communication critical thinking and attention to detail and they line up closely with what the job-posting studies above describe.
Across these sources, the same picture keeps showing up: business/data analyst roles need technical skill, analytical thinking, and the ability to work with the business side, all at once. What none of this tells us yet is which of those skills matter most specifically in apparel retail, or how close our own skills already are to that bar. That gap is what this project is built to close.

text:
Where to Focus Skill Building
Power BI and SQL are the two most market-demanded skills in our sample, each showing up in 7 of 19 postings. They are also our team’s weakest areas relative to that demand. That gap lowers skill fit scores on the scorecard directly, since Power BI and SQL are not among the four skills counted toward skill fit. In priority order:

Power BI. The single most consistent gap across all four team members. Every member self-rated at 3 or below on the market’s joint highest demand skill.
SQL. Equally in demand, with more room between team members. Zech rates Advanced, the rest rate Intermediate.
Python. Requested in 5 of 19 postings, also rated low across our team.

Closing the Power BI and SQL gaps would raise skill fit scores on the scorecard itself. Those are the two most frequently listed skills missing from the postings currently scoring lowest on skill fit, including the TJX and Foot Locker roles.
By person: Alyssa and Ankita should complete a Power BI learning path before the Module 5 deadline, then move to SQL practice against our own filtered dataset. Sara should prioritize Power BI first given her lowest team rating on it, building on her existing Excel strength. Zech should focus on Power BI’s data modeling features, building on his existing SQL proficiency.

How to Use This Product Going Forward

Re-run the Opportunity Scorecard as new postings come in. Employer signal and skill demand can shift as hiring continues.
Treat the Opportunity Score as a starting point, not a verdict. It has not been checked against real hiring outcomes, and its three components should be read individually, not just as one combined number.
Use the skill priorities above, Power BI, then SQL, then Python, to guide coursework and self-study for the rest of the semester. Those are the skills most likely to move a posting from low-scoring to high-scoring.

title: Final Recommendations
text:
Limitations
Our sample is 19 postings from a narrowly filtered search: NAICS 458, known apparel and fashion employers. These recommendations describe this specific sample, not the broader apparel analytics job market.
Salary and remote work data were usable for only 4 of 19 postings each, so neither recommendation above can account for compensation or remote work preferences with much confidence.
The scorecard’s equal weighting of skill fit, accessibility, and employer signal is a modeling choice, not a validated weighting scheme. See Final Analytics for the full discussion of that limitation.

We convert each skill’s share of the 19 postings into a target proficiency level, then compare that target against the team average to flag priority.

    "Power BI": "Power BI",
    "SQL": "SQL (Programming Language)",

    "Stakeholder Mgmt": "Stakeholder Management",

demand_pct = {label: skill_counts.get(full, 0) / len(clean_df) * 100 for label, full in skill_map.items()}

def target_level(pct):
    if pct >= 30:
        return 5
    elif pct >= 20:
        return 4
    elif pct >= 10:
        return 3
    else:
        return 2

def priority(gap):
    if gap >= 1.5:
        return "High"
    elif gap > 0:
        return "Moderate"
    else:
        return "Low"

gap_summary = pd.DataFrame({
    "Skill": list(df_skills.columns),
    "Market Demand": [f"{demand_pct[s]:.1f}%" for s in df_skills.columns],
    "Target Level": [target_level(demand_pct[s]) for s in df_skills.columns],
    "Team Average": df_skills.mean().round(2).values,
})
gap_summary["Gap"] = (gap_summary["Target Level"] - gap_summary["Team Average"]).round(2)
gap_summary["Priority"] = gap_summary["Gap"].apply(priority)
gap_summary = gap_summary.sort_values("Gap", ascending=False).reset_index(drop=True)

Power BI and SQL sit furthest to the right, Data Analysis furthest to the left, the same story the table tells, just faster to read at a glance.
Comparing market demand against team proficiency helps show where we’re well-covered and where the gaps actually are both as a team and for each of us individually.
As a team Power BI is our largest gap. It’s tied for the most in-demand skill in the market showing up in 7 of 19 postings but has the lowest average proficiency on the team at 2.75. SQL is the other most requested skill at 7 of 19 postings and fares a bit better with a team average of 3.25. Python is requested in 5 postings and also comes in low at 2.75. Excel and Data Analysis are the opposite story: both are in demand in the market and also where we rate ourselves strongest so there’s no real gap to address there.
Breaking this down by person the picture looks a bit different for each of us:

Alyssa rates Intermediate (3) in Power BI SQL and Python the three most in-demand technical skills and rates strongest in Data Analysis Stakeholder Management and Project Management (all 4). Ankita follows a similar pattern also rating a 3 in Power BI SQL and Python with Digital Marketing as her lowest rating (2). Since Power BI and SQL have the highest market demand those are the higher priority gaps for her compared to Digital Marketing.
Sara has the largest individual gap in Power BI rating herself a 2 (Beginner) the lowest score on the team for the most in-demand skill and she’s also lowest on Python (2). She’s strongest in Excel (5) and rates highly in Digital Marketing Stakeholder Management and Data Analysis (all 4).
Zech has the strongest overall technical profile on the team rating Advanced (4) in SQL Project Management and Data Analysis. His lowest ratings are Power BI and Digital Marketing (both 3) making Power BI his one real gap relative to the market’s top-requested skill.

title: Skill Gap Analysis
text:
Improvement Plan
Based on the gaps above our individual priorities are:

Alyssa and Ankita should prioritize Power BI and SQL before the Module 5 deadline, since both are currently at Intermediate despite being the two most requested skills in the market. Microsoft’s free Power BI learning path along with practicing SQL queries against the team’s own filtered dataset would tie skill-building directly to the project.
Sara should prioritize Power BI first, before the Module 5 deadline, since it’s the team’s lowest individual rating on the market’s most in-demand skill, followed by Python. Given her existing strength in Excel a Power BI path that builds on familiar spreadsheet concepts (for example Microsoft’s Excel-to-Power-BI transition materials) may be the fastest route in.
Zech should prioritize Power BI before the Module 5 deadline, the one skill where his rating trails his otherwise strong technical profile. Given his existing SQL proficiency focusing on Power BI’s data modeling features is a natural next step since those build on relational concepts he already knows.

Across the team Power BI is the most consistent gap since every member rated it at 3 or below while it ties for the highest market demand. Team members with relatively higher proficiency in a given skill (for example Zech in SQL and Sara in Excel) can informally support others when related project tasks come up rather than treating skill-building as separate from the coursework itself.
